:::{#thm-affine-map-props}
#### Linear maps and affine maps

1. An affine map $f(\vx) = \matr{A}\vx + \vec{b}$ (@def-affine-map)
   sends $\vzero$ to its offset: $f(\vzero) = \vec{b}$.
2. An affine map $f(\vx) = \matr{A}\vx + \vec{b}$ is linear (@def-linear-map)
   if and only if $\vec{b} = \vzero$.
3. Every linear map is affine.
4. An affine map determines its matrix and offset:
   if also $f(\vx) = \matr{A}'\vx + \vec{b}'$ for all $\vx$,
   then $\matr{A}' = \matr{A}$ and $\vec{b}' = \vec{b}$.

:::

::: proof

**Part 1.** First, $\matr{A}\vzero = \vzero$: for each $i$,

$$
\ba
(\matr{A}\vzero)_i
&= \sum_{j=1}^{p} a_{ij} \cd 0
&& \text{(@def-matvec-mult)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^{p} 0
&& \text{(any number times } 0 \text{ is } 0 \text{)}
\\&= 0
&& \text{(a sum of zeros is } 0 \text{)}
\ea
$$

Then

$$
\ba
f(\vzero)
&= \matr{A}\vzero + \vec{b}
&& \text{(@def-affine-map)}
\\&= \vzero + \vec{b}
&& (\matr{A}\vzero = \vzero)
\\&= \vec{b}
&& \text{(adding } \vzero \text{ changes no entry; @def-vector-addition)}
\ea
$$

**Part 2.**
If $\vec{b} = \vzero$, then $f(\vx) = \matr{A}\vx + \vzero = \matr{A}\vx$,
which is linear by @thm-matrix-map-linear.
Conversely, if $f$ is linear, then $f(\vzero) = \vzero$ by @thm-linear-map-zero,
and $f(\vzero) = \vec{b}$ by part 1,
so $\vec{b} = \vzero$.

**Part 3.**
If $f$ is linear, @thm-linear-map-matrix gives a matrix $\matr{A}$
with $f(\vx) = \matr{A}\vx = \matr{A}\vx + \vzero$,
which is @def-affine-map with $\vec{b} = \vzero$.

**Part 4.**
By part 1, applied to each formula, $\vec{b} = f(\vzero) = \vec{b}'$.
Then $\matr{A}\vx = f(\vx) - \vec{b} = \matr{A}'\vx$ for all $\vx$,
so $\matr{A}$ and $\matr{A}'$ are both matrices of the linear map
$\vx \mapsto f(\vx) - \vec{b}$ (linear by @thm-matrix-map-linear),
and the uniqueness in @thm-linear-map-matrix gives $\matr{A}' = \matr{A}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-linear-affine-terminology}
#### "Linear" in this site, and in machine learning and statistics

This site uses "linear" only in the sense of @def-linear-map,
so by @thm-affine-map-props a function with a nonzero offset is affine but not linear.
For functions of one variable, this is the same split as
[affine](algebra.qmd#def-affine-function) $a x + b$
versus [linear](algebra.qmd#def-linear-function) $a x$
on the algebra page.
(The algebra page writes these as $m x + b$ and $m x$;
here $m$ already names the number of outputs.)

Machine learning and statistics often call any function of the form
@eq-linear-scalar "linear",
as in a *linear layer* of a neural network or a *linear model*,
and call the offset $b$ the **bias** (machine learning)
or the **intercept** (statistics).
A model with an intercept is affine in $\vx$
but linear in its coefficients $(b, \vec{w})$,
and that is the sense of "linear" in "linear model":
it stays linear in the coefficients even when the inputs are transformed,
as in polynomial regression.
Appending a constant $1$ to $\vx$ also makes the model linear in the augmented input,
with $b$ as the coefficient on that entry.

:::
